passage:
Friday
Tarun lent me his chemistry notes again. That's the whole of Unit 4 now, plus the night he explained moles to me on the phone at 10 pm. I keep thinking: what have I given him back? Nothing. I bought him a cold drink once. That doesn't count.
Today he asked if I could film his cricket trial on Sunday. Of course I said yes, right away, even though Sunday is my cousin's engagement. I'll just go late.
The weird part: at lunch he joked, "You owe me like ten pizzas, Nilesh." Everyone laughed. I laughed. But something went tight in my chest, like there's a bill growing that I can never clear. I don't want to feel like that about my best friend.

qa.q: Which unit's chemistry notes has Tarun lent?
qa.a: Tarun has lent the whole of Unit 4.

qa.q: What made something go tight in Nilesh's chest at lunch?
qa.a: Tarun's joke about owing ten pizzas made the help feel like a growing bill that Nilesh can never clear 😔

qa.q: Nilesh said yes to Sunday straight away, despite the engagement. What might have been a better choice?
qa.a: Nilesh could have offered another time; saying yes out of guilt, at a cost to family, turns friendship into a ledger.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel if he knew his pizza joke landed so heavily?
qa.a: Tarun would probably be surprised and sorry, since he likely meant it as teasing between best friends, not a real debt.

grounding: A teenager who has received a friend's notes and help feels guilty about not repaying, and senses the friendship turning into a ledger.

passage: All through the board exams, Ramesh had lent Jatin his bicycle, walking the three kilometres to the kasba school himself so Jatin could reach the far exam centre on time. Now the exams were over, and Jatin could not stop thinking about it. Each time he passed Ramesh's courtyard, he felt the bicycle bell ringing somewhere in his chest. So on Sunday he turned up at dawn to help Ramesh's family bring in the wheat. He worked till his palms blistered. At noon Ramesh handed him a tumbler of water and said, "Why are you killing yourself? It was a cycle, not a loan." Jatin didn't know what to say. He only knew that until he'd paid something back, he couldn't quite look Ramesh in the eye.

qa.q: How far did Ramesh walk so Jatin could use the bicycle?
qa.a: Ramesh walked the three kilometres to the kasba school.

qa.q: Why did Jatin work till his palms blistered?
qa.a: He felt guilty and in Ramesh's debt for the bicycle, and couldn't look him in the eye until he'd paid something back.

qa.q: When Ramesh says "It was a cycle, not a loan", what choice does Jatin have?
qa.a: Jatin could accept the gift as freely given, say a real thank-you, and help in future because he wants to rather than to clear a debt.

qa.q: How does Ramesh seem to see the favour?
qa.a: Ramesh sees it as a simple kindness between friends and seems uneasy that Jatin is treating it like a debt.

grounding: A teenager who received a friend's bicycle for the exams feels a strong pull to repay it and cannot rest until he has.

passage: When Zanele's laptop broke in March, Alejandro lent her his old one for the whole term. He even set it up for her and showed her how to recover a lost essay. Zanele, fifteen, was grateful. At first. Then every time she opened the lid in her room in Johannesburg, she felt a small weight. What had she given back? A packet of biscuits. That didn't count. When Alejandro asked her to help him with his history project, she said yes at once, though she had two tests that week. At lunch he joked, "Zanele owes me a kidney." Everyone laughed, and so did she. But on the walk home the joke stayed with her, and she felt a flash of resentment she didn't like, as if their friendship had turned into a bill she could never pay.

qa.q: What did Alejandro lend Zanele?
qa.a: He lent her his old laptop for the whole term.

qa.q: What did Zanele feel when she heard Alejandro's joke?
qa.a: She felt a flash of resentment and guilt, as if their friendship had become a bill she could never pay.

qa.q: What could Zanele try instead of silently counting her debt?
qa.a: She could thank Alejandro openly, help him with his history project in a way that suits her time, and tell him the joke made her uneasy.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see the laptop he lent?
qa.a: He may see it as a simple kindness and not realise his joke made Zanele feel she owed him.

grounding: A teenager who received a big favour feels a pull to return it, and guilt and resentment when she cannot, as the friendship starts to feel like a ledger.

passage: In the school's coding lab, Arohi had spent three lunch breaks helping Parul fix her robot's sensor for the science exhibition. Parul, fourteen, won second prize. She thanked Arohi twice and bought her a samosa. Still, it didn't feel enough. On Monday Arohi said, "Can you do my library duty on Thursday? I've got dance practice." Parul said yes, though Thursday was her only free period. The next week Arohi asked again. Parul said yes again. By the third time, Parul felt a knot in her stomach when she saw Arohi coming. She liked Arohi. She owed her. But each favour seemed to open a new line in some book only she could see. Sitting alone at the library desk, stamping books, she wondered when she would be allowed to say no.

qa.q: What did Arohi help Parul fix?
qa.a: Arohi helped Parul fix the robot's sensor for the science exhibition.

qa.q: Why did Parul feel a knot in her stomach when she saw Arohi coming?
qa.a: She felt she still owed Arohi for the robot help, so she felt guilty saying no and a bit resentful at being asked again.

qa.q: What could Parul say to Arohi to protect the friendship?
qa.a: She could thank Arohi warmly again and say she can't take library duty every week, so helping doesn't become a debt she keeps paying.

qa.q: How might Arohi see the favours asked of Parul?
qa.a: Arohi may see them as small, friendly swaps and not realise Parul feels trapped by owing Arohi.

grounding: A teenager who received help feels obliged to keep repaying it, and guilt and resentment grow as the friendship starts to feel like a ledger.

passage: Varun, you asked why I always return favours so fast? Let me tell you. I'm Ira nani. When I was fifteen, in Allahabad, my friend Kamala lent me her history notes for the whole year, because I was sick for two months. I passed because of those notes. Then, before the finals, Kamala asked me to help her with maths. I was busy preparing my own exams and said, "Later." Later never came. She failed maths. I kept telling myself it wasn't my fault. But every time I saw her, I felt guilty, as if I owed her a debt I hadn't paid. She stopped sitting with me. Years later I found her address and wrote to say sorry. She wrote back: "I never kept a list." I had. That was the sad part.

qa.q: How long was Ira sick?
qa.a: Ira was sick for two months.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling every time she saw Kamala?
qa.a: Ira felt guilty, as if carrying an unpaid debt.

qa.q: Why was writing to Kamala years later a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It let Ira finally admit the unpaid favour and apologise, easing the guilt and showing the ledger was mostly in Ira's head.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt when Ira said "Later"?
qa.a: Kamala may have felt hurt and let down, having helped Ira all year.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling the pull to repay a friend's help and years of guilt when she didn't, showing how reciprocity binds and can become a ledger.

passage: The power had gone out across the colony the night before the physics exam, and Sachin, fifteen, was studying by a flickering candle. All term, Nitin had given him his neat notes whenever Sachin missed class for cricket. Now his phone buzzed: Nitin. "Can you explain optics? I'm totally lost." Sachin's battery was at ten percent, and he hadn't finished optics himself. He typed, "Sorry, I'm stuck too," then deleted it. He felt a hot knot of guilt; Nitin had never once said no to him. But helping would take an hour he didn't have. He stared at the candle. Then he called, and they worked through three diagrams over the phone until the battery died. Sachin went to bed with less revision but lighter in his chest.

qa.q: What had Nitin given Sachin all term?
qa.a: Nitin had given him his neat notes.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he deleted his message?
qa.a: Sachin felt a hot knot of guilt, aware that Nitin had never said no to him.

qa.q: Why did Sachin's choice to call feel right to him?
qa.a: It let him repay Nitin's help, easing the guilt and keeping the friendship balanced, even at a cost to his own revision.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel after the call?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt relieved and grateful that Sachin returned the help when he needed it.

grounding: A teenager who received notes all term feels a pull to return the favour and guilt if he doesn't, in a power cut the night before an exam.

passage: Tanuja, sixteen, had helped Chaitanya with maths every evening after school for a whole term, sitting at the colony's library table in Hyderabad. He'd scored ninety in the half-yearly. Now she needed help with her chemistry project, and he was the only one who knew how to use the lab software. "Can you help me Saturday?" she asked. "I'm busy. Maybe next week," he said, not looking up from his phone. Next week, he said the same. Tanuja started noticing every time he asked her for a maths answer. Each question felt like another coin in a box he never paid back. She felt resentful and a little stupid. At dinner she told her mother, "I think I've been keeping a list of everything I've done for him." Her mother said, "Then maybe it's time to tell him, not just count."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya score in the half-yearly?
qa.a: He'd scored ninety in the half-yearly.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Chaitanya kept saying "next week"?
qa.a: Tanuja felt resentful and a little foolish, as if her help was never going to be returned.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's mother suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She suggests telling Chaitanya directly instead of silently counting, which could clear the resentment and give him a chance to reciprocate.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the situation?
qa.a: Chaitanya may not even realise how much Tanuja has done or how unfair his "next week" feels to her.

grounding: A teenager who helped a friend all term feels resentment when he doesn't return the favour, noticing that reciprocity has become a ledger.

passage:
In Class 10, Bidisha helped me pass maths. I'm Sarita. She stayed back every Wednesday for three months and explained algebra until I stopped panicking.
I passed. And then something strange happened: I couldn't relax around her. I kept thinking, I owe her. When she asked me to help with her science project, I said yes before she finished the sentence, even though I had exams too.
Then in March she asked if I could come to her cousin's wedding. I couldn't go. I felt awful for weeks, as if I'd broken a promise.
Looking back, she never asked for anything back. The ledger was all in my head. It made our friendship feel heavy.

qa.q: How long did Bidisha stay back every Wednesday?
qa.a: She stayed back every Wednesday for three months.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel after missing the cousin's wedding?
qa.a: Sarita felt awful and guilty for weeks, as if a promise had been broken.

qa.q: What could Sarita have told Bidisha?
qa.a: Sarita could have said how grateful the help felt, and asked whether Bidisha wanted anything back, instead of carrying a hidden debt.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have seen Sarita's quick yeses?
qa.a: Bidisha may have been pleased but puzzled, not knowing Sarita felt a heavy debt.

grounding: Shows a teenager who received help from a friend feeling a strong pull to repay it, and guilt when unable, turning friendship into a ledger.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B
Raghav tutored Arnab in maths all term, and Arnab passed. Since then, I've noticed a change.
Arnab brings Raghav a chocolate every day. He carries Raghav's bag. Today he gave Raghav the answer to a science question in class, which I stopped.
When I spoke to Arnab after class, he said, "I owe him. I'll never finish paying him back." He looked upset, not happy.
Raghav told me separately that he feels awkward. "I don't want chocolates. I just want my friend back."
Tomorrow I'll sit with them together and help them talk about it.

qa.q: What does Arnab bring Raghav every day?
qa.a: Arnab brings Raghav a chocolate every day.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he said he'd never finish paying Raghav back?
qa.a: He felt upset and burdened, carrying the help like a debt he couldn't repay.

qa.q: How could the teacher's meeting with both boys help?
qa.a: It could let them say how they feel, so Arnab sees that Raghav helped as a friend and doesn't want payment.

qa.q: How does Raghav feel about the chocolates?
qa.a: Raghav feels awkward and misses the friendship, wanting his friend back instead of gifts.

grounding: Shows a teenager who received help feeling a heavy pull to repay it, turning the friendship into a ledger, noted by a teacher.

passage:
Monday
Arnab asked me today if I could help him with his chemistry project this weekend. I said I had cricket practice. True, but I could have skipped it. The whole walk home I felt sick about it. When I was ill for two weeks in August, Arnab photocopied every single note for me and even wrote a summary. I passed because of him. So why didn't I say yes? Maybe because it feels like I have to. Like there's a bill. And then Arnab said, "No problem, I'll manage," and that made it worse. I'm going to text him. I'll help on Sunday. But I hate that part of me is doing it to feel even again.
Wasim

qa.q: What did Arnab do when Wasim was ill in August?
qa.a: He photocopied every single note and even wrote a summary.

qa.q: What is Wasim feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Wasim feels guilty and sick about saying no, and a little resentful that the help feels like a bill to be paid.

qa.q: What could Wasim say to Arnab to make the friendship feel less like a ledger?
qa.a: Wasim could say honestly that the August notes meant a lot and that the help now comes from friendship, not from repaying a debt.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when Wasim says he has cricket practice?
qa.a: Arnab may feel a little let down but hides it with "No problem, I'll manage", not wanting to make Wasim feel obliged.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who received help from a friend feeling the pull to repay it and guilt when it stays unpaid.

passage: All through the winter term, Manjula had let Pallavi use her cycle to ride to the kasba school while Manjula took the bus with her aunt. Pallavi was grateful. She brought Manjula guavas from the tree, braided her hair before exams, and still felt she owed more. One evening at the handpump, Manjula said lightly in front of the other girls, "Pallavi rides my cycle, so she'll carry my water today." The girls laughed. Pallavi carried the pot home, her face hot. She kept thinking: was every guava a payment? That night she told her mother she wanted to walk to school from now on. Her mother said, "Tell Manjula how that felt, instead." Pallavi lay awake, unsure what she wanted.

qa.q: What did Pallavi bring Manjula from the tree?
qa.a: Guavas.

qa.q: Why was Pallavi's face hot as she carried the pot home?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and resentful that Manjula mentioned the cycle in front of the girls, making the kindness feel like a debt.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's mother suggest, and why could it be better than walking?
qa.a: Telling Manjula how it felt; it gives the friendship a chance to be fixed instead of ending the favour silently.

qa.q: How might Manjula have meant her comment?
qa.a: Manjula said it lightly and may have meant it as a joke, not realising it made Pallavi feel owed and exposed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who received a favour feeling bound to repay it and hurt when it is treated as a debt.

passage: By Advent, Jana had corrected eleven of Jamal's German essays. She never asked for anything; she just returned them with green ink and a smiley face. His grades went up. And every time he saw green ink, something in his chest tightened. He owed her. On the Friday before the Christmas market opened, Jana asked if he could help carry her grandmother's boxes on Saturday. He had promised his uncle a shift at the bakery. "Sorry, I can't," he said, and watched her smile go small. That night he lay awake doing sums: eleven essays, zero favours. On Monday he brought her a whole bag of his uncle's pastries. Jana looked puzzled. "Jamal, it's not a shop," she said. "You don't have to pay me back."

qa.q: How many essays had Jana corrected by Advent?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Jamal feel after saying he couldn't help on Saturday?
qa.a: He felt guilty and in debt, lying awake counting eleven essays against zero favours returned.

qa.q: What could Jamal do instead of paying Jana back with pastries?
qa.a: He could tell Jana honestly that he felt he owed her and offer help when she really needs it, letting the friendship be give-and-take rather than a ledger.

qa.q: How does Jana see the bag of pastries?
qa.a: Jana is puzzled, since she helped as a friend and never thought of it as a debt.

grounding: A teenager helped repeatedly by a friend feels a pull to repay and guilt when he cannot, turning the friendship into a ledger.
